missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to recall typical values of speed for a person walking, running and cycling as well as the typical values of speed for different types of transportation systems.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson gives one transport speed only. keyPoints[1].content says 'Each type of transport has its own typical speed. A car on a motorway, at about 30 m/s, is one example.' It gives no typical values for other transport such as trains, buses, aircraft or a car in town.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to draw distance–time graphs from measurements and extract and interpret lines and slopes of distance–time graphs, translating information between graphical and numerical form.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson teaches how to interpret d-t graphs. It never teaches how to plot a d-t graph from measured distances and times, such as choosing axes, plotting points and drawing a line or curve.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: draw velocity–time graphs from measurements and interpret lines and slopes to determine acceleration
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson interprets v-t graphs only. It does not teach how to draw one from measurements.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: A vector quantity may be represented by an arrow. The length of the arrow represents the magnitude, and the direction of the arrow the direction of the vector quantity.
missing_spec_content.why: Arrow representation is taught only for force, in keyPoints[5].content: 'You can show a force as an arrow.' The scalar and vector key point (keyPoints[0]) does not say that any vector can be shown as an arrow.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to express a displacement in terms of both the magnitude and direction.
missing_spec_content.why: The only worked example gives the magnitude but not the direction. keyPoints[0].content says 'Displacement = 500m, in a direction you can find with a scale drawing.' So the student never sees a displacement written out in full with both magnitude and direction.

above_gcse.text: The five motion quantities: displacement, initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, time
above_gcse.why: The specification does not use the 'SUVAT' framework. It also defines s as distance ('distance, s, in metres, m'), while this lesson calls s displacement. This could confuse the student about what s means in v² − u² = 2as.

above_gcse.text: The area under a v-t graph equals the distance travelled.
above_gcse.why: In the specification, finding distance from the area under a v-t graph is '(HT only)'. The lesson labels counting squares as 'Higher only' but presents the area rule itself as content for every student.

above_gcse.text: On a v-t graph, the skydiver's fall shows a curve that levels off at terminal velocity. Then there is a sharp drop when the parachute opens.
above_gcse.why: Drawing and interpreting v-t graphs for objects that reach terminal velocity is '(Physics only)' in the specification. The lesson does not flag it, so Combined Science students may think it is required of them.

wrong_terms.text: Equation: v = d/t. Rearrangements: d = vt, t = d/v.
wrong_terms.spec_term: distance travelled = speed × time, s = v t (distance, s, in metres)

wrong_terms.text: (2) As speed increases, air resistance increases. The net force and the acceleration both decrease.
Terminal velocity: air resistance = weight → zero net force → constant velocity
(4) Parachute opens. Drag increases hugely, so the net force is now upward.

not_checked: All keyPoints have "diagram": null, so there were no diagrams to check.

Claims about how often or how heavily topics are examined could not be checked against the specification. Examples: keyPoints[2].tutor_note 'Area under v-t graph calculations come up as 6-mark questions'; keyPoints[4].tutor_note 'a very common 4-mark question'; keyPoints[1].tutor_note 'come up almost every year'.
